title: SIM swap: when someone takes your number
body_md:
## Your number is a spare key

Your phone says “No service.” Nothing else has changed: same desk, same coffee, and the colleague beside you, on the same carrier, is texting away. Most of the time the cause is dull: an outage, a damaged SIM, a billing problem. Once in a while it is a stranger who has just talked your carrier into moving your number to a SIM or account they control.

That is a SIM swap, or a number-port attack. From then on, calls and texts meant for you reach the attacker, sign-in and password-reset codes included. Think of your number as a spare key to your accounts, and of the swap as someone having a copy cut. A spare key is not a master key, though. The attacker may still need a password, a live session or a careless recovery flow, so control of the number does not open every account by itself. And a missing signal does not prove an attack. Treat it as a reason to check soon, not as a diagnosis.

Where your carrier offers an account PIN or a transfer lock, it can make unauthorized changes harder, but offerings and verification procedures differ from one carrier to the next. This is not the SIM PIN that locks the card itself. In the carrier’s official app, or on a number from a bill or its known website, ask three things: which changes need the account PIN, whether porting is locked separately, and how you will be alerted. Keep the carrier account’s password and recovery email secure. And never read a one-time code from your carrier to a caller who rings you claiming to be support.

## Take your accounts off SMS

Start with your primary email, because it often resets everything else. Where a service supports it, use a passkey, a security key or an authenticator app instead of SMS. An authenticator app does not depend on your number, though its code can still be phished; a passkey or security key, used properly, resists that too. Save backup codes offline or in a protected password manager, and test that you can get back into your accounts without the phone number. Some banks require SMS or phone recovery. Note that limit, and ask the bank what extra safeguards it offers. Taking your number out of every service is not always possible, nor always worth it.

## When the signal disappears

Check whether other people nearby on the same carrier are affected, and whether Wi-Fi still works. If the cause stays unclear, contact the carrier at once from another phone or a trusted internet connection, through a channel you already know. Ask whether a SIM change or port was requested. If it wasn’t yours, ask for it to be blocked or reversed, and write down the case reference.

Then, on a trusted device, open your email and financial services yourself and review recent sign-ins and transactions. If anything is unauthorized, go quickly to each provider’s fraud channel, and change credentials and end sessions as its guidance allows. Save the alerts, note the times, and keep both private.

When the number comes back, revisit your recovery methods. A replacement SIM does not undo account changes already made.

widget_config.goal: Rely less on your phone number for account recovery, and respond sensibly to a sudden loss of service without assuming it is an attack.
widget_config.today_action: In your carrier’s official app or help channel, find out whether an account PIN, a port lock or a transfer alert is available. Then check the recovery and MFA options on your primary email account.
widget_config.scope: What carriers offer, and how you report a problem, varies by country and operator. The people in the examples are invented. The FTC alert is aimed at the US and dates from 2019, so check your own carrier’s current procedure; this lesson was checked on 2026-10-20.

sources.title: FTC consumer alert: SIM swap scams
sources.scope: US consumer advice from 2019: how the scam works, the account PIN, and calling the carrier at once.

sources.title: FTC: use two-factor authentication
sources.scope: General US guidance on securing accounts; notes that text messages can be diverted in a SIM swap.

sources.title: NIST SP 800-63B: authenticators
sources.scope: US federal technical standard: a one-time password (OTP) typed in by hand does not resist phishing; WebAuthn is one example of tying sign-in to the real site’s name.

blocks.title: No service, then a carrier notice
blocks.situation: Nika’s phone shows no service. On Wi-Fi she opens her email and finds a notice from her carrier about a new SIM. Then a payment alert arrives.
blocks.analysis: Taken together, those signals justify urgent calls to the carrier and the bank, through channels she already knows, while she checks her email access on a trusted device. She notes the times, and she does not use the contact number inside a suspicious message. The payment alert alone does not prove the payment went through.

blocks.title: A planned eSIM transfer
blocks.situation: Minutes ago Pavel moved his eSIM to a replacement phone. The old handset has lost service, the new one has signal, and the carrier’s official app shows the transfer he started.
blocks.analysis: The timing, and a status he checked independently, explain the symptom. Pavel still confirms that his accounts work and that no other transfer is pending. He does not report a crime merely because the old SIM went quiet.

blocks.title: A phone goes silent at work
blocks.setup: An invented working day: your phone loses service. Whether you contact the carrier now or wait changes what you face next. No real account is used.

steps.prompt: Your phone says “no service,” while a colleague on the same carrier has full signal. What do you do first?

choices.text: Contact the carrier through a saved number or its official app, over Wi-Fi.
choices.consequence: You can learn quickly whether a SIM change exists.
choices.explanation: Check through a trusted channel before you decide what caused it.

choices.consequence: An unauthorized transfer could carry on unchecked.
choices.explanation: A quick check costs little, even if it turns out to be an outage.

steps.prompt: The carrier confirms a transfer you did not request. What do you ask for?

choices.text: Get a replacement handset and get back online.
choices.consequence: The unauthorized transfer, and the access it gave, stay in place.
choices.explanation: A new phone does not correct the carrier’s records.

choices.text: Have it blocked or reversed, secure the carrier account and get a case reference.
choices.consequence: You may get the number back, and you have a record of what happened and when.
choices.explanation: Only the carrier can undo the transfer, and the case reference shows when you reported it.

steps.prompt: Next morning there is still no signal. You reach the carrier through its official channel, and it confirms a transfer you did not request. What do you ask for now?

choices.text: Get a replacement handset and get back online.
choices.consequence: After a lost day, the unauthorized transfer is still unresolved.
choices.explanation: A new phone does not correct the carrier’s records.

choices.text: Have it blocked or reversed, secure the carrier account and get a case reference.
choices.consequence: The carrier can act, though the lost day is gone; at least you have the timeline on record.
choices.explanation: Only the carrier can undo the transfer, and the case reference shows when you reported it.

steps.prompt: Meanwhile, the bank app on a trusted laptop shows a transfer request you never made. Then the phone rings: someone from “the bank” offers to cancel it if you read out the one-time code the bank has just sent you. What do you do?

choices.text: Read the code to the caller who says they are from the bank.
choices.consequence: Another way into the account has just been handed to a scammer.
choices.explanation: A caller’s claim to be the bank is no reason to read out a code.

choices.text: Use the bank’s own fraud channel, protect your email and keep the alerts.
choices.consequence: The providers can act while the evidence is still there.
choices.explanation: Protecting your accounts and calling the bank do not have to wait until the number is back.

steps.prompt: Whether the signal returns soon or late, what follow-up lowers the risk to your accounts?

choices.text: Review your email’s recovery and MFA settings, any carrier locks on offer, active sessions and the affected accounts.
choices.consequence: You close the paths the attacker may have touched.
choices.explanation: Getting the signal back does not restore the accounts.

choices.text: Assume that getting the number back makes every account safe.
choices.consequence: Changed credentials or open sessions may survive the number’s return.
choices.explanation: Check the state of your accounts separately from the state of your SIM.

blocks.debrief: Replay both routes. Waiting costs time, but on either one you still need the number back from the carrier and, separately, a check of your accounts and your money.

questions.prompt: Your phone loses service just after you started an eSIM move yourself. What is the sound conclusion?

choices.text: Check the new device and the official transfer status before escalating.
choices.explanation: A transfer you expected can explain the symptom, so confirm it first.

choices.text: Any loss of signal is a confirmed attack.
choices.explanation: Outages and planned changes happen too.

questions.prompt: What does an account PIN actually do?

choices.text: It makes a number transfer technically impossible everywhere.
choices.explanation: No universal lock and no flawless procedure exists.

choices.text: It adds an obstacle on the carrier’s side, where it is supported, without guaranteeing safety.
choices.explanation: The carrier may demand it for changes, but procedures vary.

questions.prompt: Why move your primary email off SMS-based MFA?

choices.text: A stolen number can receive codes and resets, and a different factor removes that dependence.
choices.explanation: Email often controls the recovery of your other services.

choices.text: Because an authenticator app’s code can never be phished.
choices.explanation: A code from an app can still be typed into a fake site.

questions.prompt: The carrier has reversed a swap. What is left to check?

choices.explanation: Getting signal back does not undo changes to your accounts.

choices.text: Sessions, recovery settings and transactions on the affected services.
choices.explanation: While the attacker held the number, they could have changed the state of your accounts.
